content: Individuals are referred to health service centers for additional testing to confirm an HIV diagnosis. Those confirmed to be HIV-positive are subsequently connected to treatment and care services. In Morocco, the Association de Lutte Contre le Sida (ALCS) has been conducting HIV testing services (HTS) since 1992. Currently, it operates over 25 standalone HTS sites and 5 mobile outreach units in both urban and rural areas. HTS is provided alongside prevention education tools, psychosocial support, and prevention services tailored to key populations. Trained physicians perform testing using a single rapid HIV test, but confirmatory testing requires additional procedures, which are only available at select sites. This limitation often delays results and contributes to the loss of clients along the care continuum. In 2010, ALCS successfully lobbied the National AIDS Program (NAP) to revise the national referral policy. This advocacy led to the adoption of a new approach involving immediate post-test counseling and referral to HIV Care Units. These units perform a single venous blood draw for confirmatory testing and analyses necessary for care decisions, such as CD4 count, viral load, and screening for co-infections. Initially, physicians at these units were reluctant to comply with the new policy, refusing to provide care to referred clients, which further exacerbated client attrition. Marsa, a specialized medical center offering sexual health services, was established in 2010 and officially opened in March 2011 in Beirut. It focuses on providing services to key populations, including men who have sex with men (MSM), sex workers, and transgender individuals, without discrimination. Marsa offers a comprehensive package of services, including HTS, general medical consultations, psychosocial counseling, and dietetic counseling. Rapid test kits are used for HTS, and free testing is available for Hepatitis B and C, with rapid syphilis testing offered for a small fee. All services adhere to the latest guidance from the World Health Organization (WHO) and the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC). Marsa also conducts refresher training for staff to maintain and improve service quality. Data on clients’ sexual history and risk behaviors are collected during HTS, along with other epidemiological information, using questionnaires developed by the Lebanese National AIDS Control Programme (NAP). Between 2011 and 2015, Marsa provided health services to over 2,500 unique clients and conducted more than 4,000 HIV tests, diagnosing 69 new HIV-positive cases among MSM and 5 cases among men who have sex with both men and women. The success of Marsa’s HTS program is partly attributed to strong support from the Lebanese Ministry of Public Health and the NAP, which facilitate HTS training and manage the supply chain for rapid test kits. However, discussing sex and sexual health remains taboo in Lebanon, posing a barrier to promoting Marsa’s services. As a result, promotion relies on word-of-mouth, outreach campaigns, referrals from healthcare providers, and social media. In Pakistan, the Nai Zindagi Foundation, a non-profit organization, focuses on supporting people affected by drug use and HIV. It empowers people who inject drugs (PWID) and others living with HIV to improve their knowledge, health, and socioeconomic well-being while increasing access to essential services. HTS is recommended for all PWID, their partners, and the children of HIV-positive clients. From 2012 to 2013, approximately 17,725 PWID were registered across 19 districts in partnership with six sub-recipient organizations. Of these, 11,430 accepted HTS, with 2,839 testing HIV-positive. Among those who tested negative, 3,489 were retested three months later. Additionally, 439 partners accessed HTS, with 32 women testing HIV-positive. Due to the high risk of HIV transmission through unsafe injections, repeat testing is recommended for PWID every three months, with approximately 70% of repeat testers returning regularly. To improve access to treatment, the WHO Eastern Mediterranean Region developed a tool to assess barriers to HIV testing, linkage to care, and retention in treatment. This tool uses the cascade model and contextual qualitative data to evaluate engagement along the continuum of diagnosis and care. It also identifies opportunities to enhance access to testing, linkage, and retention in lifelong treatment. The tool has been implemented in Sudan, Pakistan, Morocco, Egypt, and Iran. Patient-level factors, such as fear of stigma, discrimination, and lack of trust in HIV services, were significant barriers to care and treatment linkage. Complex testing strategies requiring laboratory procedures and delayed results also contributed to dropouts, particularly in Iran and Pakistan. Additionally, service provider attitudes and exclusion of PWID from treatment eligibility further hindered linkage to care. In Sudan, peer navigators are being introduced to support linkage to care. In Pakistan, involving NGOs in supporting PWID adherence to treatment aims to build trust among healthcare providers and increase the likelihood of seeking treatment. In Egypt, patient flow along the HIV care continuum is being optimized to improve navigation through the system. The Adhara HIV/AIDS Association in Seville, Spain, provides community-based HTS to MSM and high-risk individuals. Services are offered in hospital infectious disease units and community centers. Lay providers are permitted to perform oral fluid-based rapid HIV testing. Clients with reactive test results are promptly linked to consultations with HIV specialists, with confirmatory testing and consultations occurring within 24 hours of diagnosis. Adhara also provides preand post-test counseling, risk-reduction counseling, and retesting recommendations based on risk levels. In Barcelona, the BCN Checkpoint, established in 2006, is a community-based center for MSM. It offers HIV testing, peer counseling, information on post-exposure prophylaxis, and linkage to medical care for HIV-positive individuals. Testing is also available for syphilis, gonorrhea, chlamydia, and Hepatitis C, with vaccinations for Hepatitis A and B. BCN Checkpoint provides education programs on HIV treatment to help clients make informed decisions and improve relationships with healthcare teams. Clients with reactive results receive immediate emotional support from HIV-positive peers and are supported throughout the confirmatory testing process. Those with negative results receive risk-reduction counseling and are invited for retesting based on their risk level. Since 2008, BCN Checkpoint has been monitoring a cohort of HIV-negative MSM to estimate HIV incidence and evaluate new prevention tools. From 2006 to 2014, the program conducted 28,687 tests for 12,540 individuals, with 942 reactive results, 34 false positives, and 23 individuals refusing confirmatory testing. One-third of newly diagnosed cases were recent infections. In Greece, the Checkpoint initiative, led by Positive Voice, provides community-based HIV, Hepatitis B, and C prevention and testing services for high-risk populations, including MSM. Services include rapid testing, peer counseling, and linkage to care. The program aims to reduce undiagnosed HIV cases, promote regular testing, and minimize stigma. From 2012 to 2015, 13,438 individuals received free HIV testing, with 304 reactive results and 303 confirmed HIV-positive cases. Clients can choose between oral fluidor blood-based tests, with most preferring the latter. Checkpoint also advocates for risk-reduction strategies and aims to eliminate HIV-related stigma through counseling and education. In Portugal, the Checkpoint LX center in Lisbon, established in 2011, provides free community-based HTS for MSM. Services include rapid testing for HIV, syphilis, and Hepatitis C, as well as sexual health counseling and linkage to care. Peer counselors and physicians identify local health needs and advocate for increased access to sexual health services.
